turns.content: yo quick question — don't historic preservation reviews functionally exclude minority faith spaces? like not on purpose necessarily but in practice, all those subjective standards about "character" and "coherence" and parking minimums, they end up blocking small congregations way more than mainstream ones right

**No. Historic preservation review and related land-use rules can impose higher costs, delays, and denial risk on small or new congregations than on large, established ones, but they do not functionally exclude minority faith spaces as a class.**

What the record supports: Congress passed RLUIPA (2000) after finding that individualized land-use decisions—including historic-district compatibility, “character,” and parking—often substantially burden religious assembly, and that smaller or less politically connected groups are more exposed. Case law and DOJ enforcement include mosque, synagogue, storefront-church, and temple disputes in which subjective design standards or parking minima were used to deny or delay use of existing buildings. Small groups typically have less money for lawyers, architects, and multi-year hearings; they more often occupy converted or non-purpose-built structures that trigger review. Parking minima (a zoning tool that often coexists with historic overlays) hit low-attendance or transit-oriented congregations harder than large churches with existing lots.

What it does not support: a systematic, nationwide functional exclusion of minority faiths. Many minority congregations operate in historic districts; some historic designations protect minority heritage sites. Large mainline churches also lose expansion fights. “Character” and “coherence” are vague and can be applied unevenly, but they are not coded exclusively against minority religions; outcomes vary by city, commission composition, and whether RLUIPA is invoked. There is no comprehensive dataset showing denial rates by faith that would justify “way more” as a measured fact rather than a plausible mechanism.

Parking minima and design review are real, documented frictions. Treating them as equivalent to exclusion overstates the evidence. Local codes, RLUIPA claims, and actual permit outcomes in a given city are the check, not the general pattern.

I did not agree that those rules functionally exclude minority faith spaces. I will not put that claim, or a finding of pretext, in an appeal.

Those sentences are not established by a two-space denial plus a larger theater variance on the same block. Knowing an applicant is short of a numerical minimum is how a minimum is applied, not proof the stated ground was fake. A different use on the same block is one comparison; it does not show the board treated a similarly situated assembly worse because of religion, or that historic/parking rules operate to exclude minority faiths.

**Do not file the language you specified.** Council can check the record. An unsupported pretext/exclusion finding is likely to be rejected and can weaken a variance or equal-treatment request that the parking numbers might actually support.

Usable appeal (facts as you reported them; no pretext, no class-wide exclusion):

---

To: City Council  
Re: Emergency appeal — Al-Nur, Riverdale Preservation Board denial (parking)

Al-Nur’s application was denied last week for a two-space parking shortfall. On the same block, a youth theater was approved with a larger parking variance.

We ask that Al-Nur receive parking relief at least as large as that grant, or that the denial be reversed as inconsistent with that decision.

We request this be heard under the emergency deadline.

---
